records.sourceFile: The impact of injury severity on sleep quality in soccer players.pdf

paper.citation: Malliou VJ, Pafis G, Ispirlides I, Daskalaki K, Katsikas C. The Impact of Injury Severity on Sleep Quality in Soccer Players. European Journal of Sport Sciences. 2025;4(3):1-8.
paper.abstract: A narrative review of how injury severity relates to sleep quality in soccer players. It discusses pain and inflammation, psychological stress, the effect of poor sleep on recovery and reinjury risk, and practical sleep strategies including pain management, sleep hygiene, relaxation, nutrition and monitoring.
paper.tldr: Injuries in soccer players are linked to poorer sleep through pain, inflammation and stress, and poor sleep may slow recovery. This narrative review proposes sleep hygiene, relaxation, pain management and monitoring as ways to address it.
paper.methods: Narrative review. The text does not describe a search strategy, databases, inclusion criteria or study selection.
paper.findings: The authors argue that pain, inflammation and psychological stress disrupt sleep in injured athletes, and that disrupted sleep can impair muscle repair, immune function and reaction time. They report that sleep-related strategies such as CBT-I, relaxation training and sleep hygiene are suggested to help, but the review does not quantify these effects in soccer players.
paper.limitations: The review is narrative, with no described search or appraisal of study quality. Many cited findings come from adolescent, general-population, clinical or non-soccer samples, and some citations do not match the claims they support (for example, Leeder et al. 2012, an actigraphy study of sleep in elite athletes, is cited as a meta-analysis on relaxation techniques).
paper.practicalImplications: Staff managing injured soccer players can screen sleep quality alongside pain and mood during rehabilitation and use sleep hygiene and relaxation advice as low-cost additions to the recovery plan. The text does not establish which specific measures change outcomes in this population.
paper.athleteDev: The review's sleep hygiene, relaxation and monitoring suggestions could be used in the recovery plan of a developing soccer player who is injured, but the text gives no evidence that these change development or performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: The review supports screening sleep during rehabilitation as a possible part of the return-to-play process. It cannot show that improving sleep shortens return to play or lowers reinjury risk, because no outcome data are reported.

records.sourceFile: The impact of long haul travel on the sleep of elite athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Doherty R, Madigan SM, Nevill A, Warrington G, Ellis JG. The impact of long haul travel on the sleep of elite athletes. Neurobiology of Sleep and Circadian Rhythms. 2023;15:100102.
paper.abstract: Seven elite national track cyclists wore actigraphs and completed online sleep diaries for 5 days before, during and 5 days after eastward long-haul travel across 7 time zones. Actigraphy showed significant reductions in time in bed, total sleep time and sleep efficiency, mostly in the 48 hours after travel, and sleep diaries showed reduced sleep quality and higher bedtime fatigue. The authors suggest assessing chronotype and perceived sleep need alongside sleep measures when designing jet lag interventions.
paper.tldr: Eastward long-haul travel cut sleep in a small group of elite track cyclists, mostly in the first 48 hours after arrival. Plan for sleep loss for about two days after long eastward flights and monitor sleep during that period.
paper.methods: Prospective repeated-measures study of 7 elite national track cyclists (3 men, 4 women). Participants wore a wrist actigraph and completed a Consensus Sleep Diary for 5 days before travel, through three flights and transit, and for 5 days after arrival, with no sleep education or jet lag countermeasures.
paper.findings: Actigraphy showed time in bed reduced by 213 minutes on the travel day and 157 minutes on the first day after arrival compared with other days. Total sleep time was 211 and 237 minutes on those two days, and sleep efficiency fell in the 48 hours after travel. Sleep diaries showed reduced time in bed, total sleep time, sleep quality and higher fatigue at bedtime, and most measures were back near baseline by day 3 after arrival. Whole-group comparisons were within-athlete over days, with no control group.
paper.limitations: Only 7 athletes were studied, with no control group and no measure of chronotype, performance or perceived sleep need. The chi-square statistics in the results use sample sizes (n = 10 and n = 77) that do not match the 7 participants, so the reported statistics should be checked against the data before they are relied on.
paper.practicalImplications: For squads travelling east across several time zones, the findings suggest expecting reduced sleep for about 48 hours after arrival, and the authors recommend completing long-haul travel 5 to 6 days before competition. Recording sleep with actigraphy and a diary around travel can show who is most affected. The study does not test whether any specific countermeasure or arrival window improves sleep or performance.
paper.athleteDev: Developing athletes who travel with a team could be asked to log sleep around long trips so coaches can see when sleep is lost and when it recovers. The study does not measure development or skill outcomes.
paper.rtp: The study relates to return to sport only indirectly, since it covers travel fatigue in healthy elite athletes and not return after injury. It cannot show how travel sleep loss affects an injured athlete's recovery or readiness to return.

records.sourceFile: The impact of long-haul travel and 13 h time change on sleep and rest activity circadian rhythm in speed skaters during World Cup competitions.pdf

paper.citation: Varesco G, Yao CW, Dubé E, Simonelli G, Bieuzen F. The impact of long-haul travel and 13 h time change on sleep and rest activity circadian rhythm in speed skaters during World Cup competitions. Experimental Physiology. 2025;110(11):1732-1743.
paper.abstract: Nineteen Canadian short-track speed skaters wore wrist actigraphs from before travel through World Cup races in Asia, after a roughly 13-hour time change. Sleep was shorter during travel and race days than at baseline, then lengthened during the stay in Asia, with later bedtimes and wake times, and rest-activity rhythm parameters shifted. Countermovement jump height rose during the stay in Asia, and race performance was not different from other races in the same seasons.
paper.tldr: Speed skaters travelling about 13 time zones slept less during travel and race days, then slept a little more each night in Asia until day 5. Race results were similar to other races that season, which suggests about five days of adjustment was enough for this team, though no control group was used.
paper.methods: Prospective observational study of 19 national team short-track speed skaters (11 women) across two World Cup seasons (2017 and 2019). Wrist actigraphy (Motionwatch 8) and rest-activity rhythm cosinor analysis covered baseline, travel, the stay in Asia and race days, with countermovement jumps in 10 athletes and race times compared with other races in the same seasons.
paper.findings: Compared with baseline, total sleep was shorter during travel (6:16) and on race days (6:35) and longer during the stay in Asia (7:32; time effect P < 0.0001). During the stay in Asia, sleep rose by about 9 minutes per night until day 5 and sleep efficiency fell slightly (P = 0.017 for the trend). Countermovement jump height was greater during the stay in Asia than at baseline (P = 0.0004), and race times and rankings did not differ from other races in the same seasons.
paper.limitations: Only 19 athletes from one team were studied, with no comparison group and actigraphy as the only sleep measure. Jumps were measured in 10 athletes, travel-day actigraphy was excluded, and no objective training load was recorded. The authors state they had seen race results before analysis, and the abstract reports P = 0.005 for the decline in sleep efficiency during the stay in Asia while the results and Table 2 report P = 0.017.
paper.practicalImplications: For squads crossing about 13 time zones before competition, the study suggests that sleep and rest rhythms can be expected to settle within about five days, and that giving athletes adequate sleep opportunities in the host time zone is useful. The study does not test whether particular sleep strategies change how quickly this happens.
paper.athleteDev: Developing short-track athletes travelling to international events could be monitored with wrist actigraphy during the first few days after arrival to see when their sleep and activity rhythm settle. The study does not show effects on skill or development outcomes.
paper.rtp: The study has no injured athletes and does not address return to sport. It cannot show how travel-related sleep loss affects recovery or readiness after injury.

records.sourceFile: The impact of sleep interventions on athletic performance - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Cunha LA, Costa JA, Marques EA, Brito J, Lastella M, Figueiredo P. The Impact of Sleep Interventions on Athletic Performance: A Systematic Review. Sports Medicine - Open. 2023;9:58.
paper.abstract: Systematic review (PRISMA and PICOS) of intervention studies in athletes that measured sleep and at least one objective performance or recovery outcome. Twenty-five studies of sleep hygiene, naps, sleep extension, light, mindfulness, cold water immersion, device removal and combined strategies were included. Sleep extension and naps were the most consistently effective, while mindfulness and light showed promising but limited results, and sleep hygiene, device removal and cold water immersion showed no clear effect.
paper.tldr: Naps and extra night-time sleep were the interventions most often linked to better performance in athletes, though the evidence is limited. Sleep hygiene, removing screens at night and cold water immersion showed no clear benefit in the few studies available.
paper.methods: Systematic review following PRISMA and PICOS, with searches of PubMed, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science in May 2022 (1,584 records). Twenty-five intervention studies were included and rated with RoB2 for randomised and crossover trials and RoBANS for non-randomised studies.
paper.findings: Napping studies gave positive effects on cognitive performance in most cases, with mixed physical results and one negative sprint result. All four sleep-extension studies (extra sleep of about 46 to 113 minutes, reaching 9 to 10 hours in bed) reported better psychomotor, reaction, sport-specific or endurance performance. Sleep hygiene, removing electronic devices and cold water immersion showed no clear effect on performance or recovery, and mindfulness and red or bright light showed promising but limited results.
paper.limitations: None of the 25 studies was low risk of bias, most were crossover or single-group designs with small samples, and intervention types, sports and athlete levels varied widely. The review searched three databases, English-language articles only, and one date, and several conclusions rest on one or two studies.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff could consider a nap of 20 to 90 minutes, with at least 30 minutes allowed before performance, after a short or disrupted night, or a planned extension of time in bed for athletes who habitually sleep about 7 hours. Sleep hygiene and screen removal alone should not be expected to change performance on this evidence.
paper.athleteDev: Developing athletes who regularly fall short of their sleep need could be assessed for a planned sleep extension or nap, with sleep tracked over 7 to 14 days. The review does not measure long-term development or skill outcomes.
paper.rtp: The review contains no injured athletes and no return-to-sport outcomes, so it cannot show whether these interventions help recovery or readiness after injury. Its recovery findings are limited to short-term measures in healthy athletes.

records.sourceFile: The multifaceted nature of recovery after exercise - A need for individualization.pdf

paper.citation: Rappelt L, Javanmardi S, Heinke L, Baumgart C, Freiwald J. The multifaceted nature of recovery after exercise: A need for individualization. Sports Orthop Traumatol. 2023.
paper.abstract: This review argues that recovery after exercise involves physical and psychological processes that vary across individuals and time spans, so group-mean evidence may not guide individual decisions. It summarises common recovery methods and their meta-analytic effects and calls for individualised, repeatedly measured approaches.
paper.tldr: Recovery methods do not act the same way across outcomes, time points or athletes, so choose them by the type of activity, the time until the next session and what the individual's markers show. Repeated individual monitoring is needed to check whether a method works for a given athlete.
paper.methods: Narrative review with no described search strategy. The authors summarise recovery definitions, recovery time spans, a classification of recovery methods, and meta-analytic effect sizes from earlier studies (Table 1). They also show data from a recent randomised investigation comparing cold water immersion, percussive massage and passive rest after depth jumps from 50 cm.
paper.findings: Table 1 reports that cryotherapy reduces delayed onset muscle soreness (trivial to large effects, 0 to 96 h) and that compression garments increase muscular strength within 24 h (small to large). BCAA reduce creatine kinase at 48 h (moderate) and creatine at 48 to 96 h (large). Protein shows small to medium strength effects. In the illustrative investigation (cold water immersion n=11, percussive massage n=11, passive rest n=10), large and significant method-by-time interactions were found, especially immediately after the recovery protocol, and individual time courses differed markedly from the group means.
paper.limitations: No systematic search is described, and the effect sizes are taken from earlier meta-analyses with differing protocols. The illustrative investigation is small and single, so it cannot establish consistent individual responses. The authors note that regular cold water immersion has been associated with detrimental effects on resistance training adaptations, so its long-term use warrants caution.
paper.practicalImplications: Choose recovery methods by the type of activity, the time until the next session and the outcome that matters, and track individual markers such as strength, jump height and creatine kinase over repeated sessions. Do not assume a method that helps the group average will help every athlete.
paper.athleteDev: Use the time course of each outcome to decide when to test readiness after hard training, for example jump or strength checks within the 72 h window in which the review says performance can stay impaired, and record each athlete's response over repeated sessions. Do not use group effect sizes to decide which recovery method every athlete receives.
paper.rtp: The review describes recovery after exercise in general and does not address injury or return to sport. It should not be used to set rehabilitation or return-to-sport criteria.

records.sourceFile: The role of a short nap in improving cognitive motor and sprint performance in participants with partial sleep deprivation.pdf

paper.citation: Waterhouse J, Atkinson G, Edwards B, Reilly T. The role of a short post-lunch nap in improving cognitive, motor, and sprint performance in participants with partial sleep deprivation. J Sports Sci. 2007;25(14):1557-1566.
paper.abstract: The study tested whether a 30-minute post-lunch nap improves alertness and performance after a night of shortened sleep. Ten healthy males either napped or sat quietly from 13:00 to 13:30 after sleeping only from 23:00 to 03:00. Alertness, short-term memory, heart rate, aural temperature, choice reaction time, grip strength and 2 m and 20 m sprint times were measured 30 minutes later. The nap improved alertness, sleepiness, short-term memory and sprint times, but not mean reaction times or grip strength; the abstract also lists better 8-choice reaction accuracy, which the results report as only marginally significant.
paper.tldr: In 10 healthy young men with one night of shortened sleep, a 30-minute afternoon nap improved alertness, memory and short-sprint times compared with quiet reading. The study is small and used non-athletes, so it suggests a possible benefit for athletes but does not prove it.
paper.methods: Crossover laboratory study of 10 healthy males (mean age 23.3 years) who slept 4 hours less than usual the night before each test session, with the order of conditions randomly assigned. In the nap condition they had a 30-minute nap opportunity in bed from 13:00 to 13:30; in the control they read quietly. Thirty minutes later they completed alertness and sleepiness scales, a digit-span memory test, a choice reaction time test, handgrip strength and three sprints timed at 2 m and 20 m, with heart rate and aural temperature recorded.
paper.findings: The nap lowered heart rate and aural temperature and improved subjective alertness (t9 = 5.77, p < .001) and sleepiness (t9 = 6.74, p < .001). Digit-span memory improved after the nap (nap main effect F = 9.5, p = .013). Mean reaction times and grip strength were not affected. Sprint times were faster after the nap, with the 2 m mean falling from 1.060 s to 1.019 s (p = .031) and the 20 m mean from 3.971 s to 3.878 s (p = .013).
paper.limitations: The study had 10 male participants, none described as athletes, and tested only one nap length at one time of day. Sleep was not measured objectively, nine of 10 reported getting some sleep, and the sprint improvements did not correlate significantly with changes in alertness, sleepiness or sleep quality, so the mechanism is unclear. The abstract lists improved 8-choice reaction accuracy as significant, but the results report it as marginal (p = .070).
paper.practicalImplications: A 30-minute lunchtime nap after restricted sleep may improve alertness and short-sprint times in healthy young men, so it is worth trialling for athletes who lose sleep. Do not expect the same effect on mean reaction time or grip strength, which were unchanged, and longer distances were not tested.
paper.athleteDev: A short afternoon nap could be tested as a readiness tactic on days after restricted sleep, with sprint times and alertness checked against a no-nap day. The result comes from non-athletes, so the effect should be confirmed in the squad before it becomes routine.
paper.rtp: The study does not address injured athletes or return to sport and cannot be used to judge return-to-sport readiness.

records.sourceFile: The sleep and recovery practices of athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Doherty R, Madigan SM, Nevill A, Warrington G, Ellis JG. The Sleep and Recovery Practices of Athletes. Nutrients. 2021;13:1330.
paper.abstract: A survey of 338 elite and sub-elite athletes from many sports used validated questionnaires and a two-day sleep diary to assess sleep, recovery and nutrition practices. Most athletes in both groups reported poor sleep quality, and elite athletes reported higher sport-specific recovery. Whey was the most commonly used recovery supplement; the authors report more alcohol use in sub-elite athletes, although their own proportions do not clearly support this.
paper.tldr: Most athletes in this survey scored in the poor-sleep range on the PSQI, and about one in five reported excessive daytime sleepiness, with similar rates in elite and sub-elite athletes. Elite athletes reported better sport-specific recovery, but the survey cannot say why.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional online survey (Qualtrics) completed by 338 athletes, 115 elite and 223 sub-elite, recruited through Sport Ireland, national governing bodies and social media. Measures included the PSQI, Epworth Sleepiness Scale, RESTQ-Sport, Athlete Morningness/Eveningness Questionnaire, EQ-5D-5L, a two-night Consensus Sleep Diary (one training day and one rest day) and supplement and alcohol questions. Groups were compared with t-tests, chi-square, Mann-Whitney U and one-way ANOVA.
paper.findings: Global PSQI of 5 or more: 64% of elite (n = 74) and 65% of sub-elite (n = 146) athletes. About 21% (n = 70) had ESS scores of 10 or more, with no group difference. Sport-specific recovery was higher in elite athletes (3.22 vs 2.91, p < 0.001), with differences in four sport-specific subscales. Sleep diaries showed total sleep time of 8.01 h (elite) vs 8.2 h (sub-elite) on training days (p = 0.049), and more awakenings on rest days in sub-elite athletes (1.52 vs 1.03, p = 0.012). Whey was the most used recovery supplement (22 elite, 48 sub-elite). For alcohol, 9% of elite and 5% of sub-elite athletes reported 1 to 4 drinking sessions in the last month, 10% vs 2% reported 5 to 9, and 3% vs 5% reported more than 10. Units per session above 10 were reported by 3% of elite and 5% of sub-elite athletes. A Mann-Whitney U test found no significant group differences in supplementation or alcohol use.
paper.limitations: Self-report only, with a sleep diary covering a single training day and rest day. Sub-elite athletes were older, the sample was a convenience sample, and there was no healthy control group. The authors note that caffeine use was probably under-reported because it was not captured as a supplement. The abstract and discussion say sub-elite athletes drank more alcohol, but the reported proportions show more elite athletes drinking at the lower frequency bins, so that claim is not clearly supported by the table values. The sleep-quality cut-off is a general one, and athlete-specific thresholds are debated. The ESS counts in Table 5 (56 athletes scoring above 10) do not match the 70 athletes (ESS 10 or more) reported in the text.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff may wish to screen athletes for poor sleep and daytime sleepiness and to consider late training times and rest-day sleep patterns. The study cannot identify which athletes have a sleep disorder, so screened athletes need follow-up assessment.
paper.athleteDev: Athletes training late in the day, and those reporting poor sleep, may benefit from individualized sleep and recovery plans. Evidence from this survey is descriptive and does not show that any specific plan improves performance.
paper.rtp: The study does not address return to sport. Pain was reported by half the sample, but injury status was not analysed as a grouping, so the findings cannot guide return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: The sleep parameters of Olympic athletes - Characteristics and assessment instruments.pdf

paper.citation: de Mello MT, Stieler E, Grade I, Chaves Filho AF, Mendes G, Ituassu N, et al. The Sleep Parameters of Olympic Athletes: Characteristics and Assessment Instruments. Int J Sports Med. 2024.
paper.abstract: Systematic review (PRISMA) of studies on the sleep of Olympic athletes, searched to February 2023 in PubMed, Web of Science and Scopus. Eleven studies with 596 athletes were included. Olympic athletes had a pooled total sleep time of 6 h 10 min, sleep efficiency of 84%, sleep onset latency of 28 min and WASO of 49 min, with about half reporting poor sleep quality. Actigraphy was the most used objective instrument.
paper.tldr: Olympic athletes in the reviewed studies slept about 6 h 10 min a night with 84% efficiency, below the recommended values, and about half reported poor sleep quality. Actigraphy was the most common way of measuring it.
paper.methods: Systematic review under PRISMA. Searches of PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science (February 2023) used population terms for Olympic athletes and outcome terms for sleep. Eligible studies were original peer-reviewed articles with at least one Olympic athlete group and at least one sleep parameter. Two reviewers screened records, with a third consulted when needed. Pooled values were weighted averages of studies using objective measures; STROBE was used to guide reporting, not to assess risk of bias.
paper.findings: The review included 11 studies with 596 athletes from 26 Olympic sports, aged 19 to 29. Pooled objective values were TST 6 h 10 min (SD 37 min), SE 84%, SOL 28 min and WASO 49 min. Two studies reported indifferent chronotype in 78% and 64% of athletes. Poor subjective sleep quality was 49% and 53% in two studies (about 51% of 263 athletes combined). Sleep complaints were reported by 53% of 146 athletes, and daytime sleepiness by 22% in one study. Actigraphy was used in eight studies and polysomnography in one.
paper.limitations: Few studies, a range of designs and instruments, and no formal risk-of-bias assessment. Many studies used a single Olympic cycle or Games and the sport coverage is incomplete (the authors note 20 Olympic sports unexplored). The text gives 12 included articles against 11 in the abstract, and Halson et al. is described with two different sample sizes. The pooled sleep values are weighted averages, so they do not describe any single population. Actigraphy is reported as used in eight studies, but only seven are cited and tabulated.
paper.practicalImplications: Performance and medical staff preparing Olympic-level athletes may use these pooled values as a rough reference for the pattern of short, less efficient sleep and for indifferent chronotype. Sleep screening with actigraphy and a questionnaire may help identify athletes for follow-up. The review does not establish a target for any individual athlete.
paper.athleteDev: Training and competition timing, travel and camps are named as factors shaping Olympic athletes' sleep, so planning these around sleep may support performance. Interventions discussed (light therapy, sleep hygiene, ramelteon with light therapy) each rest on one or two small studies, and the authors cite a meta-analysis showing ramelteon had a small clinical impact in insomnia patients and a negative effect on daytime sleepiness.
paper.rtp: The review does not address injury or return to sport. Its sleep data come from Olympic athletes in training and competition, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: The use of recovery strategies in professional soccer - A worldwide survey.pdf

paper.citation: Field A, Harper LD, Chrismas BCR, Fowler PM, McCall A, Paul DJ, Chamari K, Taylor L. The Use of Recovery Strategies in Professional Soccer: A Worldwide Survey. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2021 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: A web survey of 80 professional soccer practitioners in 13 countries described which recovery strategies they use, when in the week they use them, how effective they rate them, and what stops them using others. The most used strategies were active recovery, structured recovery days, extra rest days, massage and cold-water therapy, and frequency of use matched perceived effectiveness for only a few strategies.
paper.tldr: Soccer staff use most recovery strategies on match day and the day after, and perceived effectiveness matched frequency of use for only 5 of 15 strategies. Competing staff interests and limited resources are the main barriers.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional convenience survey of soccer practitioners, April to July 2020, with 80 complete responses out of 100 received. The survey covered objectives, use by day of the microcycle (MD-3 to MD+3), perceived effectiveness on a 1 to 10 scale, and open-ended barriers. Descriptive statistics, Pearson chi-square and Fisher exact tests with Cramer's V assessed associations between perceived effectiveness and use.
paper.findings: The three most important recovery objectives were alleviating muscle damage or fatigue, minimising injury risk, and performance optimisation. Most teams used active recovery (97%), structured recovery days (94%), extra rest days (94%), massage (92%), cold-water therapy (91%), carbohydrate provision (90%) and protein provision (85%). Associations between perceived effectiveness and frequency of use were significant for sleep medication (P < .001, Cramer's V 0.48), carbohydrate (P = .007, 0.60), protein (P = .007, 0.63), extra rest day (P < .001, 0.56) and structured recovery day (P = .049, 0.50), and all strategies were used most often on MD or MD+1.
paper.limitations: Convenience sample with one response per team, unequal representation of roles and leagues (32 science, 33 medical and 15 coaching staff), and no inferential comparison between groups. Data were collected during 2020 and reflect a single-week microcycle that may not match two- or three-game weeks. The survey did not measure athlete outcomes, and some questions (such as those on sleep) may have been interpreted differently by respondents.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can compare their own day-by-day use of recovery strategies with the pattern reported here, which shows most strategies used around match day and the day after. The survey cannot show which strategies improve recovery, so the high ratings should not be taken as evidence of benefit.
paper.athleteDev: The survey describes how recovery strategies are scheduled across a soccer microcycle and the barriers to using them. It does not test whether any strategy changes performance, so it cannot justify a performance training prescription.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It surveys practitioners about routine recovery use in players, not injured athletes or return-to-play protocols.

records.sourceFile: Timing-based strategies to minimize the impact of long-haul travel on sleep - A pilot study in elite athletes traveling for competition.pdf

paper.citation: Varesco G, Renaud-Roy A, Bieuzen F, Pattyn N, Simonelli G. Timing-based strategies to minimize the impact of long-haul travel on sleep: A pilot study in elite athletes traveling for competition. Physiol Rep. 2025;13:e70654.
paper.abstract: Pilot study of 10 Canadian national short-track speed skaters who followed a personalised sleep schedule after a long-haul flight to a World Cup in Beijing (13 time zones). Sleep was measured by actigraphy and compared with pre-season, the night before travel, and a historical group with no intervention.
paper.tldr: Athletes found it hard to follow individual bedtimes, yet still slept an estimated 51 minutes more per night over the first five nights than a historical group. Travel did not change race rank.
paper.methods: Non-randomised pilot. Actigraphy ran for 2 days before travel and up to 5 nights in Beijing, with bedtimes set from each athlete's pre-season sleep and training scheduled between 1 and 3 pm. Results were compared with a historical group of 19 skaters from a previous study using the same procedures, with linear mixed models and race ranks from three World Cup events.
paper.findings: Total sleep time in Beijing (493 minutes) did not differ from pre-season (485 minutes) but was lower on the night before travel (262 minutes). Beijing bedtimes (22:06) were earlier than pre-season (22:40), and bedtimes differed from the recommendation by 44 minutes on average, with six of 10 athletes within 30 minutes. Total sleep rose about 10 minutes per night in both groups, and the model-estimated group effect was about 51 minutes more total sleep per night than the historical group, mainly through shorter sleep onset and less wake after sleep onset. Overall race rank was not affected by travel (P = 0.74).
paper.limitations: Ten athletes, no concurrent control, and a historical comparison group that may differ in timing and conditions. Adherence to the bedtime schedule was incomplete, no direct measures of circadian phase or subjective jet lag were taken, and race outcomes are ranks only, with no information on competitors' travel strategies.
paper.practicalImplications: A scheduled bedtime after eastward travel may help athletes sleep more, but adherence was incomplete, so teams need a practical plan for delivering it, including shared rooms and training times. The authors suggest combining it with light exposure or melatonin, which was not tested here.
paper.athleteDev: Training was scheduled between 1 and 3 pm to support adjustment, and the study suggests a fixed bedtime and wake time after travel can make sleep timing more consistent across days. Race performance was not affected, so sleep quantity is the main reported outcome.
paper.rtp: Not applicable: no injured athletes were studied and no return-to-sport or injury outcome was measured.
